issues.legal_issue: A share that became separate property upon partition devolves by succession under the Hindu Succession Act, including to qualifying female heirs, rather than by survivorship.
material_facts: After the death of the family ancestor, a notional partition under Section 82 of the Madhya Bharat Land Code gave his son, grandson, and widow separate shares.
The son’s share thereby became his separate property and he died after the Hindu Succession Act came into force, leaving a wife and daughter.
The High Court increased the daughter’s share in the family property, and the Supreme Court upheld that decision.
issues.conclusion: The son’s property devolved by succession, not survivorship, and the surviving female heirs were entitled to the shares provided by the Hindu Succession Act.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act addresses a Mitakshara coparcener who dies after the Act comes into operation without testamentary disposition of his undivided share. Its proviso provides for the devolution of that interest where the deceased leaves a daughter or another female Class I heir. Here, the earlier partition had made the son’s share separate property, and its devolution was by succession. The court also relied on Section 82 of the Madhya Bharat Land Code in finding that the earlier partition had occurred. No earlier case was cited on this issue.

rule.if: partition_suit and prior_partition_made_share_separate and property_holder_died_after_succession_law_commenced and female_class_one_heir_survived

predicates.partition_suit: The proceeding sought division of family property among persons claiming shares in it.
predicates.prior_partition_made_share_separate: An earlier partition allotted the property holder a share as separate property.
predicates.property_holder_died_after_succession_la: The holder of the separate share died after the applicable succession law had come into operation.
predicates.female_class_one_heir_survived: A female heir within the relevant class of heirs survived the property holder.

issues.definition: When a partition proceeding concerns a separate share created by an earlier partition and its holder died after the succession law commenced leaving a female heir in the relevant class, the property devolves by succession, including to female heirs.

issues.legal_issue: A will is not proved unless its execution is established in accordance with the statutory requirements for testamentary documents.
material_facts: The trial court accepted wills propounded in support of the appellant’s claimed shares, but the High Court found their execution unproved.

The evidence concerning the first will included contradictions between the witnesses and scribe; one attesting witness was related to the appellant, and the scribe was connected to the appellant’s family.
The evidence concerning another will led the High Court to find that its execution had been manoeuvred and was not acceptable.
The Supreme Court found no reason to interfere with the High Court’s factual findings on the wills.
issues.conclusion: The wills were not proved, and the High Court’s findings rejecting them were left undisturbed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, the propounder must call at least one attesting witness to prove execution. The propounder must establish the testator’s signature, testamentary capacity, sound and disposing state of mind, understanding of the disposition, and free will; suspicious circumstances must be explained to the court’s satisfaction. The judgment also refers to the provisions of the Indian Succession Act and applies Savithri v. Karthyayani Amma, (2007) 11 SCC 621, for these requirements.

predicates.will_proof_dispute: The proceeding required the court to decide whether a will had been proved.
predicates.will_propounded: A party relied on a will to support a claimed entitlement to property.
predicates.attesting_witness_not_reliably_establish: The evidence of the attesting witness or other execution evidence did not reliably establish that the will was executed as alleged.

issues.definition: When a will is relied on in a proceeding and the attesting-witness evidence does not reliably establish its execution, the will is not proved.

issues.legal_issue: A female heir’s claim to partition of a dwelling house is not barred by the dwelling-house restriction when the house is not wholly occupied by family members.
material_facts: A married daughter sought partition of family property that included a dwelling house.
Evidence showed that a portion of the house was let out and that the bungalow was also let for marriage purposes, for which rent was collected.
The High Court found that the house was not wholly occupied by family members and held it available for partition; the Supreme Court upheld that finding.
issues.conclusion: Because the dwelling house was not wholly occupied by family members, it was available for partition and the daughter could claim her share in it.
issues.legal_principle: Section 23 of the Hindu Succession Act imposed the relevant restriction on a female heir’s right to seek partition of a dwelling house only where it was wholly occupied by family members. The court held that the restriction did not apply on the facts because the house was not wholly so occupied. No earlier case was cited on this issue.

predicates.partition_suit: The proceeding sought division of family property among persons claiming shares in it.
predicates.female_heir_seeks_house_partition: A female heir claimed partition of a dwelling house forming part of the family property.
predicates.dwelling_house_not_wholly_occupied_by_fa: The dwelling house was not wholly occupied by members of the family, including because some of it was let or used for other purposes.

issues.definition: When a female heir seeks partition of a dwelling house in a partition proceeding and the family does not wholly occupy it, the house is available for partition.
